A small thing that costs people credibility, and almost nobody is taught it. If a rate goes from four per cent to six per cent, that is not a two per cent increase. It is an increase of two percentage points, and it is also a fifty per cent increase. Those are three different numbers describing exactly the same movement, and if you pick the wrong one the person listening will either think it is tiny or think it is enormous. I have watched a room approve something because somebody said two per cent, when the honest sentence was that the rate went up by half. So here is the rule I use. Say the two numbers first, from and to. Four to six. Then say the movement, and say which kind it is. Nobody has ever been criticised for being that clear, and it takes one extra second.

When I present numbers to people who do not work with them all day, I use three sentences per figure and never more. The first sentence is the number and what it is a proportion of. Not just three point four. Three point four times our monthly fixed costs. The second sentence is the comparison, and I always give the direction and the size together: that is up from two point nine last year, so roughly twenty per cent higher. The third sentence is what it means, in words that have nothing to do with accounting: at this level we cover our costs by the middle of the month. Three sentences. And if I cannot say the third one, I have learned that it is because I do not understand the figure yet, and no slide is going to fix that for me.
